items.stem: Define the term "dietary fibre".
items.answer: Indigestible plant material that adds bulk and keeps food moving through the gut
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: indigestible plant material that adds bulk and keeps food moving through the gut. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a teenager needs more energy each day than a 70-year-old of the same sex.
items.answer: Teenagers are growing and usually more active, so their cells need more energy and materials for new tissue.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Teenagers are growing and usually more active, so their cells need more energy and materials for new tissue. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A balanced diet means eating equal amounts of every food group." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A balanced diet contains all nutrients in the right proportions for your needs – more carbohydrate and vegetables, less fat and sugar.
items.markingKey: A balanced diet contains all nutrients in the right proportions for your needs – more carbohydrate and vegetables, less fat and sugar. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student needs 10000 kJ per day but eats food containing 11200 kJ per day. Calculate the difference and state what will happen to their body mass over time if this continues.
items.answer: 1200 kJ per day extra; they will gain body mass
items.markingKey: M1 11200 − 10000 = +1200 kJ; A1 1200 kJ; B1 they will gain mass (excess stored as fat).

items.stem: Yusuf plans to investigate how the vitamin C content of orange juice changes when it is boiled for different times. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: volume of DCPIP (1 cm³); concentration of DCPIP; same carton of juice; shaking after each drop
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: volume of DCPIP (1 cm³) – more DCPIP needs more vitamin C; concentration of DCPIP – stronger DCPIP needs more juice; same carton of juice – brands differ in vitamin C; shaking after each drop – mixing ensures the endpoint is seen. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: A student eats crisps and fizzy drinks for lunch every day. Describe which nutrients are missing or in excess, and suggest and justify a better lunch.
items.answer: Excess: fat, salt and sugar (risk of obesity, tooth decay, high blood pressure); lacking: protein (growth), fibre (constipation), vitamins and minerals (e.g. vitamin C, iron, calcium). Better: wholemeal sandwich with chicken or beans, fruit, vegetables, water or milk – provides starch for energy, protein, fibre, vitamins and calcium.
items.markingKey: Excess: fat, salt and sugar (risk of obesity, tooth decay, high blood pressure); lacking: protein (growth), fibre (constipation), vitamins and minerals (e.g. vitamin C, iron, calcium). Better: wholemeal sandwich with chicken or beans, fruit, vegetables, water or milk – provides starch for energy, protein, fibre, vitamins and calcium.

items.stem: Lack of vitamin C causes which deficiency disease?
items.answer: Scurvy
items.markingKey: A. Bleeding gums, slow healing.

items.stem: Distinguish between malnutrition and starvation.
items.answer: Malnutrition is any unbalanced diet – too much or too little of some nutrients; starvation is a severe lack of food energy overall.
items.markingKey: Malnutrition is any unbalanced diet – too much or too little of some nutrients; starvation is a severe lack of food energy overall. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why eating too much saturated fat can be harmful.
items.answer: It can raise blood cholesterol, which can build up in arteries and increase the risk of heart disease, and excess energy is stored as fat (obesity).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It can raise blood cholesterol, which can build up in arteries and increase the risk of heart disease, and excess energy is stored as fat (obesity). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which James Lind and scurvy (1747) shows one of the first controlled trials.
items.answer: Lind gave groups of sick sailors different treatments; those given oranges and lemons recovered quickly. It showed a dietary cause of scurvy (lack of vitamin C) and led to the Royal Navy issuing citrus juice.
items.markingKey: Context (Lind gave groups of sick sailors different treatments; those given oranges and lemons recovered quickly.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It showed a dietary cause of scurvy (lack of vitamin C) and led to the Royal Navy issuing citrus juice. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to one of the first controlled trials.

items.stem:
Amara measured the volume of fruit juice needed to decolourise 1 cm³ of DCPIP after the juice had been stored for different numbers of days.

Storage time / days | Volume of juice / cm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 1.3 | 1.3 | 1.3
2 | 2.1 | 2.1 | 2.0
4 | 2.7 | 2.8 | 2.8
6 | 3.5 | 3.4 | 3.7
8 | 4.4 | 4.5 | 4.2

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: More juice is needed to decolourise DCPIP the longer the juice is stored, so its vitamin C content falls with time. Vitamin C is slowly broken down by oxygen (oxidised) during storage, so each cm³ of juice contains less vitamin C.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: More juice is needed to decolourise DCPIP the longer the juice is stored, so its vitamin C content falls with time.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Vitamin C is slowly broken down by oxygen (oxidised) during storage, so each cm³ of juice contains less vitamin C.

items.stem: "Sugary drinks should be taxed to reduce obesity." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: A sugar tax helps, but must be part of wider education and healthy-food policies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: taxes have reduced sugary-drink sales in several countries; manufacturers reduced sugar content; money raised can fund school sport. Arguments against: hits poorer families harder; people may switch to other high-sugar foods; obesity has many causes. Supported judgement: A sugar tax helps, but must be part of wider education and healthy-food policies. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: What is the main job of the large intestine?
items.answer: Absorbing water from undigested food
items.markingKey: Absorbing water from undigested food. Faeces form there.

items.stem: "Bile is an enzyme that digests fat." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Bile contains no enzymes; it emulsifies fat into droplets so lipase can work faster, and neutralises stomach acid.
items.markingKey: Bile contains no enzymes; it emulsifies fat into droplets so lipase can work faster, and neutralises stomach acid. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why large food molecules such as starch must be digested.
items.answer: They are too large and insoluble to pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood; small soluble molecules can be absorbed. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are too large and insoluble to pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood; small soluble molecules can be absorbed. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Nia placed visking tubing containing starch and amylase in water at 37 °C and measured the glucose concentration of the outside water over time.

Time / min | Glucose concentration / mg/dm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
5 | 22 | 22 | 22
10 | 41 | 43 | 42
15 | 62 | 64 | 59
20 | 85 | 79 | 81
25 | 99 | 97 | 101

Calculate the mean glucose concentration when the time was 25 min.
items.answer: 99.0 mg/dm³
items.markingKey: M1 (99 + 97 + 101) ÷ 3; A1 99.0 mg/dm³ (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Food moves 30 cm through the oesophagus in 8 seconds by peristalsis. Calculate the average speed in cm/s.
items.markingKey: M1 speed = distance ÷ time = 30 ÷ 8; A1 3.75 cm/s.

items.stem: Using William Beaumont and Alexis St Martin (1820s) as an example, explain observing digestion.
items.answer: Beaumont studied a patient with a hole into his stomach from a gunshot wound, tying food on strings into the stomach and removing it later. He showed that gastric juice digests food chemically, not just by grinding – though the ethics of the study are questioned today.
items.markingKey: Context (Beaumont studied a patient with a hole into his stomach from a gunshot wound, tying food on strings into the stomach and removing it later.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: He showed that gastric juice digests food chemically, not just by grinding – though the ethics of the study are questioned today. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to observing digestion.

items.stem: Describe the journey of a mouthful of a cheese sandwich through the digestive system, naming where each nutrient is digested and absorbed.
items.answer: Mouth: chewing, amylase in saliva starts starch digestion. Oesophagus: peristalsis. Stomach: acid and protease (pepsin) start protein digestion; churning. Small intestine: bile emulsifies fat; pancreatic amylase, protease, lipase finish digestion to sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol; absorbed through villi into blood. Large intestine: water absorbed; fibre egested as faeces.
items.markingKey: Mouth: chewing, amylase in saliva starts starch digestion. Oesophagus: peristalsis. Stomach: acid and protease (pepsin) start protein digestion; churning. Small intestine: bile emulsifies fat; pancreatic amylase, protease, lipase finish digestion to sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol; absorbed through villi into blood. Large intestine: water absorbed; fibre egested as faeces.

items.stem: Alessia plans an investigation into how the pH affects the digestion of egg white protein by pepsin. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (pH of the solution (1, 2, 4, 6, 8 using buffers)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The muscular tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach"?
items.answer: oesophagus
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of oesophagus.

items.stem: Explain how villi are adapted for absorption.
items.answer: They give a huge surface area, have walls one cell thick for a short diffusion distance, and a good blood supply that carries absorbed food away, keeping a concentration gradient.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They give a huge surface area, have walls one cell thick for a short diffusion distance, and a good blood supply that carries absorbed food away, keeping a concentration gradient. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between mechanical digestion and chemical digestion.
items.answer: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces (teeth, stomach churning); chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.
items.markingKey: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces (teeth, stomach churning); chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Food is digested in the stomach and that is where it is absorbed." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The stomach starts protein digestion, but most digestion finishes, and almost all absorption happens, in the small intestine.
items.markingKey: The stomach starts protein digestion, but most digestion finishes, and almost all absorption happens, in the small intestine. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Yusuf plans to investigate how the pH affects the digestion of egg white protein by pepsin. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: volume and concentration of pepsin; temperature (37 °C water bath); volume of egg-white suspension; the same observer and white background
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: volume and concentration of pepsin – more enzyme digests faster; temperature (37 °C water bath) – enzyme activity depends on temperature; volume of egg-white suspension – more substrate takes longer; the same observer and white background – judging clearness. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Kwame wants to find out how the pH affects the digestion of egg white protein by pepsin. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does pH of the solution affect time for a cloudy egg-white suspension to become clear?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (pH of the solution (1, 2, 4, 6, 8 using buffers)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (time for a cloudy egg-white suspension to become clear) in a question form.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Gastric band surgery is a good solution to obesity."
items.answer: Surgery can help severely obese patients, but diet and lifestyle change are needed for most people.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large weight loss; reduces type 2 diabetes. Arguments against: surgical risks and side effects; does not change eating habits; expensive for health services. Supported judgement: Surgery can help severely obese patients, but diet and lifestyle change are needed for most people. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the pH affects the digestion of egg white protein by pepsin. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Put 5 cm³ egg-white suspension and 2 cm³ buffer into tubes at each pH; warm in a 37 °C water bath for 5 min; add 1 cm³ pepsin, start the stopwatch; record time until clear against a black card; repeat three times; include a control with boiled enzyme.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (acid buffers are irritants – wear eye protection; enzymes can cause allergies – avoid skin contact). Model: Put 5 cm³ egg-white suspension and 2 cm³ buffer into tubes at each pH; warm in a 37 °C water bath for 5 min; add 1 cm³ pepsin, start the stopwatch; record time until clear against a black card; repeat three times; include a control with boiled enzyme.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "active site".
items.answer: The part of an enzyme where the substrate fits
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the part of an enzyme where the substrate fits. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why enzyme reactions slow down at low temperatures.
items.answer: Molecules have less kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate collide less often and fewer successful collisions happen each second.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Molecules have less kinetic energy, so enzyme and substrate collide less often and fewer successful collisions happen each second. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Enzymes are killed by high temperatures." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Enzymes are not alive so cannot be killed; they are denatured – the shape of the active site changes.
items.markingKey: Enzymes are not alive so cannot be killed; they are denatured – the shape of the active site changes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Freya measured how long a protease took to clear a cloudy milk suspension at different pH values.

pH | Time to clear / s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 100 | 95 | 100
2 | 69 | 67 | 69
3 | 98 | 99 | 97
4 | 187 | 184 | 181
5 | 327 | 326 | 326

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The time is shortest at pH 2 and increases as pH moves away from 2 in either direction. This protease (like pepsin) has an optimum pH of about 2; at other pH values the shape of the active site changes, so fewer substrate molecules fit.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The time is shortest at pH 2 and increases as pH moves away from 2 in either direction.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: This protease (like pepsin) has an optimum pH of about 2; at other pH values the shape of the active site changes, so fewer substrate molecules fit.

items.stem: Using Enzymes in lactose-free milk as an example, explain enzymes in food technology.
items.answer: Lactase enzyme is added to milk to break lactose into glucose and galactose, so people with lactose intolerance can drink it. Using an enzyme outside the body solves a digestion problem for millions of people.
items.markingKey: Context (Lactase enzyme is added to milk to break lactose into glucose and galactose, so people with lactose intolerance can drink it.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Using an enzyme outside the body solves a digestion problem for millions of people. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to enzymes in food technology.

items.stem: Alessia investigated how temperature affects the time taken for amylase to digest starch. The method had this weakness: samples were tested only every 2 minutes. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: test every 30 s (or 10 s) to make the end-point time more precise
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: test every 30 s (or 10 s) to make the end-point time more precise

items.stem: What are the products of protein digestion?
items.answer: Amino acids
items.markingKey: D. Proteins are chains of amino acids.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an enzyme being denatured and an enzyme being inactive at low temperature.
items.answer: At low temperature the enzyme is just slow and will work again when warmed; a denatured enzyme has its active site permanently changed and cannot work again.
items.markingKey: At low temperature the enzyme is just slow and will work again when warmed; a denatured enzyme has its active site permanently changed and cannot work again. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between an enzyme being denatured and an enzyme being inactive at low temperature.
items.answer: At low temperature the enzyme is just slow and will work again when warmed; a denatured enzyme has its active site permanently changed and cannot work again.
items.markingKey: At low temperature the enzyme is just slow and will work again when warmed; a denatured enzyme has its active site permanently changed and cannot work again. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Tomás wants to find out how temperature affects the time taken for amylase to digest starch. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does temperature of the water bath affect time until a sample no longer turns iodine blue-black?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (temperature of the water bath (°C)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (time until a sample no longer turns iodine blue-black – tested every 30 s on a spotting tile) in a question form.

items.stem: Iodine stopped turning blue-black after 60 s when amylase digested a starch solution. Calculate the rate of reaction as 1000 ÷ time, in s⁻¹.
"Enzymes should be used in more industrial processes instead of high-temperature chemical reactions." Discuss.
items.answer: Enzymes are a greener option for many processes when conditions can be controlled.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: work at low temperatures, saving energy; specific, so fewer waste products; biodegradable. Arguments against: denatured easily by heat or wrong pH; can be expensive to produce and purify. Supported judgement: Enzymes are a greener option for many processes when conditions can be controlled. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which food test must be heated in a water bath?
items.answer: Benedict’s test for sugar
items.markingKey: Benedict’s test for sugar. About 80 °C for a few minutes.

items.stem: Distinguish between a qualitative food test and a quantitative measurement.
items.answer: A qualitative food test shows whether a nutrient is present (colour change); a quantitative measurement gives an amount, e.g. energy in kJ/g by calorimetry.
items.markingKey: A qualitative food test shows whether a nutrient is present (colour change); a quantitative measurement gives an amount, e.g. energy in kJ/g by calorimetry. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the type of nut affects the energy released when it burns, state the dependent variable and describe how Mohammed should measure it.
items.answer: temperature rise of 20 cm³ of water, used to calculate energy per gram
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: temperature rise of 20 cm³ of water, used to calculate energy per gram.

items.stem: A 0.6 g cashew nut was burned under a tube of 10 g water. The temperature rose by 27 °C. Calculate the energy released per gram of food (in J/g) and suggest why the value is lower than on the packet.
items.answer: 1890 J/g; energy was lost to the air and the tube (and burning was incomplete)
items.markingKey: M1 energy = 10 × 4.2 × 27 = 1134 J; M1 ÷ 0.6; A1 1890 J/g; B1 heat lost to surroundings / incomplete combustion.

items.stem: Plan an investigation to compare the energy content of three snack foods by burning them. Include a calculation and two ways to reduce energy losses.
items.answer: Mass a food sample; 20 cm³ water in a boiling tube clamped above it; record initial temperature; ignite food on a mounted needle and hold under the tube until it burns out (relight if needed); record maximum temperature. Energy (J) = 20 × 4.2 × temperature rise; per gram = energy ÷ mass. Repeat three times. Reduce losses: insulate the tube/use a draught shield, keep food close to the tube, use a calorimeter with a metal can.
items.markingKey: Mass a food sample; 20 cm³ water in a boiling tube clamped above it; record initial temperature; ignite food on a mounted needle and hold under the tube until it burns out (relight if needed); record maximum temperature. Energy (J) = 20 × 4.2 × temperature rise; per gram = energy ÷ mass. Repeat three times. Reduce losses: insulate the tube/use a draught shield, keep food close to the tube, use a calorimeter with a metal can.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Biuret test"?
options: A test for lipids: shaken with ethanol then water, a cloudy white emulsion forms
An illness caused by a lack of a particular nutrient in the diet
Measuring the energy released by burning a food, using the temperature rise of water
A test for protein: the solution turns from blue to purple
items.answer: A test for protein: the solution turns from blue to purple
items.markingKey: D. "Biuret test" is a test for protein: the solution turns from blue to purple.

items.stem: "If iodine stays orange, the food contains no nutrients." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It only shows there is no starch; the food may contain sugar, protein or fat.
items.markingKey: It only shows there is no starch; the food may contain sugar, protein or fat. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.markingKey: 1 1.0 g; 1 range = max − min = 32.5 − 31.3 = 1.2 °C; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: "Calorie counting is the best way to stay healthy." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Energy balance matters, but the quality and balance of nutrients matter just as much.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: helps control body mass by matching energy in and out. Arguments against: ignores vitamins, minerals, fibre and protein; can encourage unhealthy obsession with food. Supported judgement: Energy balance matters, but the quality and balance of nutrients matter just as much. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "absorption"?
options: An enzyme that breaks down starch into maltose (sugar)
Waves of muscle contraction that push food along the gut
Describes an enzyme whose active site has changed shape so the substrate no longer fits
The movement of digested food molecules from the small intestine into the blood
items.answer: The movement of digested food molecules from the small intestine into the blood
items.markingKey: D. "absorption" is the movement of digested food molecules from the small intestine into the blood.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "vitamin"?
options: A protein that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up reactions without being used up
An enzyme that breaks down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol
A test for protein: the solution turns from blue to purple
An organic substance needed in small amounts to stay healthy, e.g. vitamin C
items.answer: An organic substance needed in small amounts to stay healthy, e.g. vitamin C
items.markingKey: D. "vitamin" is an organic substance needed in small amounts to stay healthy, e.g. vitamin C.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The molecule that an enzyme acts on"?
items.answer: substrate
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of substrate.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the same volume of water should be used each time when comparing the energy in foods.
items.answer: The temperature rise depends on the mass of water heated; using the same volume makes the comparison fair.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The temperature rise depends on the mass of water heated; using the same volume makes the comparison fair. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces (teeth, stomach churning); chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.
items.markingKey: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces (teeth, stomach churning); chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones. items.stem: Explain the difference between vitamins and minerals.
items.answer: Vitamins are organic compounds made by living things (e.g. vitamin C); minerals are inorganic elements taken from soil and water (e.g. iron, calcium); both are needed in small amounts.
items.markingKey: Vitamins are organic compounds made by living things (e.g. vitamin C); minerals are inorganic elements taken from soil and water (e.g. iron, calcium); both are needed in small amounts. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Enzymes are used up in the reaction." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Enzymes are catalysts; they are unchanged and can be used again and again.
items.markingKey: Enzymes are catalysts; they are unchanged and can be used again and again. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the emulsion test uses ethanol.
items.answer: Fats dissolve in ethanol but not in water; when water is added the fat comes out of solution as tiny droplets, making the liquid cloudy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Fats dissolve in ethanol but not in water; when water is added the fat comes out of solution as tiny droplets, making the liquid cloudy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: The stomach starts protein digestion, but most digestion finishes, and almost all absorption happens, in the small intestine.

0 | 1.3 | 1.3 | 1.3
2 | 2.0 | 2.1 | 2.1
4 | 2.8 | 2.9 | 2.8
6 | 3.7 | 3.7 | 3.7
8 | 4.3 | 4.3 | 4.4

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: More juice is needed to decolourise DCPIP the longer the juice is stored, so its vitamin C content falls with time. Vitamin C is slowly broken down by oxygen (oxidised) during storage, so each cm³ of juice contains less vitamin C.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: More juice is needed to decolourise DCPIP the longer the juice is stored, so its vitamin C content falls with time.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Vitamin C is slowly broken down by oxygen (oxidised) during storage, so each cm³ of juice contains less vitamin C.

items.stem: In an investigation into how temperature affects the time taken for amylase to digest starch, state the dependent variable and describe how Diego should measure it.
items.answer: time until a sample no longer turns iodine blue-black – tested every 30 s on a spotting tile
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: time until a sample no longer turns iodine blue-black – tested every 30 s on a spotting tile.

items.answer: 285 kJ

items.stem: Arjun writes: "If iodine stays orange, the food contains no nutrients." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It only shows there is no starch; the food may contain sugar, protein or fat.
items.markingKey: It only shows there is no starch; the food may contain sugar, protein or fat. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Gastric band surgery is a good solution to obesity."
items.answer: Surgery can help severely obese patients, but diet and lifestyle change are needed for most people.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large weight loss; reduces type 2 diabetes. Arguments against: surgical risks and side effects; does not change eating habits; expensive for health services. Supported judgement: Surgery can help severely obese patients, but diet and lifestyle change are needed for most people.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the vitamin C content of orange juice changes when it is boiled for different times. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Boil 50 cm³ samples of juice for each time and cool to room temperature; put 1 cm³ DCPIP in a test tube; add juice drop by drop from a burette or graduated pipette, shaking, until the blue colour disappears; record the volume; repeat three times for each time; calculate means.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (DCPIP is an irritant – wear eye protection; hot liquids scald). Model: Boil 50 cm³ samples of juice for each time and cool to room temperature; put 1 cm³ DCPIP in a test tube; add juice drop by drop from a burette or graduated pipette, shaking, until the blue colour disappears; record the volume; repeat three times for each time; calculate means.

items.stem: Use the lock-and-key model to explain how temperature affects the rate of starch digestion by amylase from 10 °C to 70 °C.
items.answer: Starch fits amylase active site (complementary shape). From 10 °C rate rises as particles move faster – more collisions and enzyme–substrate complexes; maximum at about 37 °C (optimum); above this vibrations change the active site shape – denatured – starch no longer fits, so the rate falls rapidly to zero by about 60–70 °C.
items.markingKey: Starch fits amylase active site (complementary shape). From 10 °C rate rises as particles move faster – more collisions and enzyme–substrate complexes; maximum at about 37 °C (optimum); above this vibrations change the active site shape – denatured – starch no longer fits, so the rate falls rapidly to zero by about 60–70 °C.

items.stem: Mohammed investigated how the type of nut affects the energy released when it burns. The method had this weakness: the nut went out and was not relit. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: relight the nut until it no longer burns and check that only ash is left

items.stem: Where is most digested food absorbed into the blood?
items.answer: Small intestine
items.markingKey: D. It has villi.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An organic substance needed in small amounts to stay healthy, e.g. vitamin C"?
items.answer: vitamin
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of vitamin.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "lipase"?
options: The breakdown of large insoluble food molecules into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed
An enzyme that breaks down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol
An inorganic element needed in small amounts, e.g. iron and calcium
A test for starch: iodine turns from orange-brown to blue-black
items.answer: An enzyme that breaks down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol
items.markingKey: B. "lipase" is an enzyme that breaks down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Biuret test and the Benedict’s test.
items.answer: Benedict’s detects reducing sugars and needs heating (blue → brick red); Biuret detects protein at room temperature (blue → purple).
items.markingKey: Benedict’s detects reducing sugars and needs heating (blue → brick red); Biuret detects protein at room temperature (blue → purple). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why large food molecules such as starch must be digested.
items.answer: They are too large and insoluble to pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood; small soluble molecules can be absorbed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are too large and insoluble to pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood; small soluble molecules can be absorbed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Fat is always bad for you." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Some fat is needed for energy storage, insulation, cell membranes and absorbing vitamins A and D; the problem is too much, especially saturated fat.
items.markingKey: Some fat is needed for energy storage, insulation, cell membranes and absorbing vitamins A and D; the problem is too much, especially saturated fat. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why each enzyme only acts on one substrate.
items.answer: The active site has a specific shape that only fits one substrate (lock and key), so other molecules cannot bind.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The active site has a specific shape that only fits one substrate (lock and key), so other molecules cannot bind. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the Benedict’s test and the Biuret test.
items.answer: Benedict’s detects reducing sugars and needs heating (blue → brick red); Biuret detects protein at room temperature (blue → purple).
items.markingKey: Benedict’s detects reducing sugars and needs heating (blue → brick red); Biuret detects protein at room temperature (blue → purple). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between absorption and assimilation.
items.answer: Absorption is the movement of digested food into the blood; assimilation is when cells use the absorbed molecules to build new substances.
items.markingKey: Absorption is the movement of digested food into the blood; assimilation is when cells use the absorbed molecules to build new substances. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kenji wants to find out how the vitamin C content of orange juice changes when it is boiled for different times. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does boiling time affect volume of juice needed to decolourise 1 cm³ of DCPIP?

items.answer: 50 s⁻¹

items.markingKey: M1 temperature rise = 34 °C; M1 energy = 20 × 4.2 × 34; A1 2856 J.

items.stem: A model small intestine is a tube 5 m long with an inside surface area of 0.5 m². Villi and folds increase the surface area by a factor of 30. Calculate the total absorbing surface area and explain why this is important.
items.answer: 15 m²; a larger surface area allows faster absorption of digested food by diffusion
items.markingKey: M1 0.5 × 30; A1 15 m²; B1 larger area → more absorption per second.

items.stem: Briefly describe James Lind and scurvy (1747) and explain what it reveals about one of the first controlled trials.
items.answer: Lind gave groups of sick sailors different treatments; those given oranges and lemons recovered quickly. It showed a dietary cause of scurvy (lack of vitamin C) and led to the Royal Navy issuing citrus juice.
items.markingKey: Context (Lind gave groups of sick sailors different treatments; those given oranges and lemons recovered quickly.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.answer: Enzymes are not alive so cannot be killed; they are denatured – the shape of the active site changes.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Probiotic yoghurts are worth buying to keep the digestive system healthy."
items.answer: Probiotics may help in specific cases, but a high-fibre balanced diet is better evidence-based value.

items.stem: "Enzymes should be used in more industrial processes instead of high-temperature chemical reactions." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Enzymes are a greener option for many processes when conditions can be controlled.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: work at low temperatures, saving energy; specific, so fewer waste products; biodegradable. items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the type of nut affects the energy released when it burns. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Weigh a nut; clamp a boiling tube containing 20 cm³ water; record the temperature; set the nut alight on a mounted needle and hold it 1 cm under the tube until it stops burning; record the highest temperature; calculate energy = 20 × 4.2 × rise and divide by mass; repeat with three nuts of each type.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (nut allergies – check before the lesson; burning food is hot – use a heat-proof mat and tie back hair). Model: Weigh a nut; clamp a boiling tube containing 20 cm³ water; record the temperature; set the nut alight on a mounted needle and hold it 1 cm under the tube until it stops burning; record the highest temperature; calculate energy = 20 × 4.2 × rise and divide by mass; repeat with three nuts of each type.
